newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Gaullists rap colleague over Le Pen dinner.
newsitem.headline: French Gaullists rap colleague over Le Pen dinner.

text.p: French Gaullists sought to distance themselves on Tuesday from a senior party colleague who dined with far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen and advocated talks with his anti-immigrant National Front.
The Gaullist RPR group in the National Assembly described last week's dinner as a private, personal and regrettable initiative by fellow-deputy Robert Pandraud.

"In any case, it does not commit our group and our movement who have a line of behaviour and intend to stick to it," they said after their weekly meeting which Pandraud, a former security minister, did not attend.
Le Pen, who advocates sending immigrants back and espouses racial inequality, has been kept at arm's length by mainstream political parties for his extremist views.

But some right-wing politicians have begun wondering aloud how to poach the Front's 15 percent share of the vote in view of the conservatives' defeat to the left in last month's parliamentary elections.
The RPR deputy secretary general, Patrick Stefanini, also said he disapproved of Pandraud's initiative, but his criticism was less than forthright.

"It was not a good idea to dine with Le Pen in the current circumstances...It will be up to the new RPR president to clearly define his positions on the issue of relations with the National Front," he told RMC radio.

Former National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, who is to take over the RPR chairmanship from ex-prime minister Alain Juppe at an emergency party congress on Sunday, said he had summoned Pandraud to a meeting next week.
The Socialist Party has suggested that Seguin, unless he fired Pandraud, would be seen as backing talks with the Front.

The Greens, partners in the ruling left-wing coalition, said the RPR, which was founded by President Jacques Chirac, was reaching out to the National Front and would bear "a heavy responsibility for allowing its xenophobic, racist and anti-Repoublican ideas lasting roots".

Both Pandraud and Le Pen have confirmed that they dined together at a Paris restaurant last week. Pandraud has said that neither the Front nor the RPR wanted to strike an alliance at present but he favoured a dialogue.
